findings.title: No tests for drain contract, signal handling, or handler isolation
findings.evidence: run() is the whole public contract (stop -> no new pulls -> in-flight jobs complete) and nothing in the diff exercises it.
findings.recommendation: Add tests: (a) stop requested while jobs are in flight still runs them all before run() returns; (b) stop set before run() pulls nothing; (c) a raising handler does not kill the worker and the remaining jobs still run; (d) source raising a non-queue.Empty exception drains then propagates. Use a fake source object with a get(timeout=...) method rather than sleeping on real wall-clock time.

findings.title: SIGINT/SIGTERM handlers are replaced process-wide and never restored, so a hung drain is uninterruptible
findings.evidence: signal handlers are installed in install_signal_handlers() and never saved/restored; once installed, a second Ctrl-C or SIGTERM during the pool drain only re-sets the Event instead of interrupting.
findings.recommendation: Save the previous handlers returned by signal.signal and restore them in a try/finally around the run() body; additionally, on a second stop request (or a counter in request_stop) restore the default handler so a hung handler can be interrupted instead of requiring SIGKILL.

findings.title: Unbounded submit gives no backpressure; pending-future queue can grow without limit
findings.evidence: the loop submits any number of jobs to the executor independently of how fast handlers finish, so a fast producer with slow handlers accumulates unbounded pending futures and memory.
findings.recommendation: Bound in-flight work: keep a set of futures and stop pulling from the source while len(pending) >= max_workers * k (retiring done futures each iteration), or pull the job inside the worker threads instead of in the dispatch loop.

findings.title: run() unconditionally installs signal handlers, so it raises ValueError off the main thread and is untestable there
findings.evidence: signal.signal is only legal in the main thread; the docstring documents the constraint but run() has no guard, so any embedder or test invoking run() from a thread fails immediately.
findings.recommendation: Only install handlers when threading.current_thread() is threading.main_thread() (guarded by hasattr(signal, 'SIGTERM') for portability), or split run() into a handler-installing wrapper and a run_loop() that is safe to call from any thread.

findings.title: Stop Event is never cleared, so a reused worker's run() silently does nothing
findings.evidence: the loop condition short-circuits on a permanently set Event, so calling run() again on the same instance returns 0 immediately without draining any queued work.
findings.recommendation: Clear the Event at the start of run() (or document the instance as single-use and raise if run() is entered twice) so a restart cannot be mistaken for a completed run.

findings.title: run() returns 0 even when jobs failed, hiding partial failure from the caller
findings.evidence: handler exceptions are only logged in _run_job and run() unconditionally returns 0, so a caller cannot distinguish a clean drain from one where every job raised.
findings.recommendation: Track a failure counter (or per-job outcomes) and return a non-zero code / expose the count when any job failed, so a supervising process can alert or retry.
